# Biological War Just Became a Bestseller. The Early-Warning System It's Looking For Is Already Under Our Feet.


[Mariana Matus](https://substack.com/@marianamatus)


Sep 22, 2026


Annie Jacobsen has a gift for making the unthinkable feel immediate. Her book


*Nuclear War: A Scenario* did that for nuclear weapons. It became an instant


*New York Times* bestseller by walking readers minute-by-minute through what an attack would actually look like. Her new one,


*Biological War: A Scenario* , does the same thing for a pandemic-as-weapon. She talked to dozens of experts to build it.


I was one of them. So were Admiral Brett Giroir and Hon. Andy Weber — two people I’ve had the honor to swap notes with for years, from very different seats at the table. A few years ago, a journalist wouldn’t have thought to call a wastewater company for a book like this. Now it’s an obvious call. That shift says a lot about where this field has gone.


Here’s the part of her scenario that really sticks with me: in a real biological event, the thing you’re short on isn’t smart people. It’s time. Doctors can only test for what they think to look for, in someone who’s already sick enough to show up at a clinic. A new or engineered pathogen doesn’t come with a warning label. By the time hospitals start noticing a pattern, the days that actually mattered are already gone. The pathogen has likely already spread.


This is where wastewater adds value to other critical data sources. Everybody flushes, whether they’re sick or not, tested or not, worried or not. Couple the ability to broadly screen for pathogens circulating in pipes with the ability to rapidly investigate anomalous detections and you get a privacy-first early signal for the whole community. That’s the entire idea behind Biobot, and it’s exactly what you’d want on hand for a scenario like the one Jacobsen writes about.


And this isn’t hypothetical: it’s already happened, twice, in the last two years. A team at Baylor College of Medicine (Dr. Anthony Maresso and Dr. Michael Tisza who run Texas’s wastewater metagenomics sequencing program) found bird flu, H5N1, in the wastewater of all ten Texas cities they were watching back in 2024. This was months before public health officials learned it was spreading among Texas cattle and infecting cattle workers. Then in January 2025, the same program spotted measles in Houston’s wastewater from just two travelers, before a single case had even been reported. That city hadn’t seen a measles signal in 31 months of testing. Two people, in a city of 2.3 million, caught by a sewer sample.


That’s an early-warning system working exactly the way you’d hope, for a disease we already understand well. Imagine what it could do for one we don’t.


So here’s what I can’t stop thinking about after reading Jacobsen’s book: the tool that would matter most in the first hours of a real biological crisis isn’t some exotic new technology. It’s something unglamorous, underfunded, and mostly treated as a nice-to-have instead of critical infrastructure. Turning wastewater monitoring into a permanent part of how we defend against biological threats is where I think this field needs to head next. It’s certainly where we’re headed.


A couple things I’d genuinely love to hear people’s take on:


If someone released a new pathogen in a busy airport tomorrow, how many days do you think it’d take wastewater monitoring to catch it, versus doctors noticing a pattern in their patients? Where does one start beating the other?


Biological warfare doesn’t have to mean some lab-made superbug. Sometimes it just means exploiting a gap that’s already there. What are the critical sentinel sites around the country that should be watched right now, but aren’t? Do you think there are pathogens that could potentially be invisible to wastewater monitoring systems?


More on that second one soon. We just wrapped a pilot testing exactly this during the 2026 World Cup, and I’ll be sharing what we found. Stay tuned.
